parts.name: Passage 1
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1.

Otters

A

Otters have long, slender bodies and short legs, a shape well suited to pushing through dense undergrowth and hunting in tunnels. An adult male may grow to about 4 feet in length and weigh up to 30 lb; females are typically smaller. The Eurasian otter’s nose is among the smallest of the otter species and has a characteristic shape resembling a shallow ‘W’. An otter’s tail, sometimes referred to as its rudder or stern, is stout at the base and tapers towards the tip, where it becomes flatter. It forms part of the animal’s propulsion system when swimming rapidly underwater. Otter fur consists of two types of hair: stout guard hairs, which form a waterproof outer covering, and dense, fine underfur, which provides insulation and helps retain body heat. The coat must be kept in good condition through regular grooming. Seawater reduces its waterproofing and insulating qualities when it penetrates the fur. This is why freshwater pools are particularly important to otters living on the coast. After swimming in the sea, they wash their coats in these pools and then squirm on the ground, rubbing themselves dry against vegetation.

B

Otters use their sense of smell when hunting on land, communicating with one another and detecting danger. Their sense of smell is thought to be similar in sensitivity to that of dogs. Otters have small eyes and are probably short-sighted on land. However, they can alter the shape of the lens in the eye, making it more spherical and thereby compensating for the refraction of light in water. In clear water and good light, they can therefore hunt fish by sight. The eyes and nostrils are positioned high on the head, allowing an otter to see and breathe while most of its body remains submerged. Underwater, it holds its legs close to the body except when steering, while the rear of the body moves in a series of vertical undulations. River otters have webbing extending along much of each digit, though not quite to the tips. Giant otters and sea otters have even more extensive webbing, whereas Asian short-clawed otters have almost none. They hunt for shrimps in ditches and paddy fields, so they do not need the same swimming speed as species that pursue prey through open water. Otters’ ears are small for streamlining, but their hearing is highly sensitive. The ears are also protected by valves that close against water pressure.

C

A number of requirements and preferences limit the habitats suitable for otters. Water is essential, and rivers must be large enough to support a healthy population of fish. Because otters are shy and wary animals, they tend to prefer territories where human activity causes relatively little disturbance. There must also be no other otter already occupying the same territory, a factor that becomes increasingly important as populations recover. Coastal otters generally have a more abundant food supply, and the ranges of both males and females may extend for only a few kilometres along the coast. A male’s range may overlap with those of two or three females. Otters will eat almost anything they can catch, and there are records of them consuming sparrows, snakes and slugs. Apart from fish, their most common prey includes crayfish, crabs and water birds. Small mammals are taken occasionally, most commonly rabbits but sometimes even moles.

D

Eurasian otters can breed at any time of year when food is readily available. In places where conditions are more severe, such as Sweden, where lakes remain frozen for much of the winter, cubs are generally born in spring. This ensures that they are well grown before severe weather returns. In the Shetland Islands, by contrast, cubs are born in summer, when fish are more abundant. Although otters are capable of breeding every year, some do not. Again, this depends partly on food availability. Other factors, such as the range of food available and the condition of the female, may also have an effect. Gestation in the Eurasian otter lasts about 63 days. By contrast, in Lutra canadensis, the embryos may undergo delayed implantation.

E

Otters normally give birth in secure dens where there is little risk of disturbance. Nests are lined with bedding such as reeds, waterside plants and grass to keep the cubs warm while the mother is away feeding. Litter size varies from one to five cubs. For reasons that are not fully understood, coastal otters tend to produce smaller litters. At about five weeks, when a cub weighs around 700 g, its eyes open. At seven weeks, cubs begin to be weaned onto solid food. At ten weeks, they leave the nest and encounter daylight for the first time. By around three months, they enter the water and begin learning to swim. At eight months, they are able to hunt, although the mother still supplies a considerable amount of food. By about nine months, the young are sufficiently independent for the mother to drive them away.

F

The decline of the British otter was recognised in the early 1960s, although its principal cause was not identified until the late 1970s. Pesticides such as dieldrin and aldrin had first been introduced in 1955 for use in agriculture and other industries. These chemicals are highly persistent and had already been linked to major declines in populations of peregrine falcons, sparrowhawks and other predators. The pesticides entered river systems and passed through the food chain, from micro-organisms to fish and finally to otters, with the concentration of the chemicals increasing at each stage. From 1962, these pesticides were gradually phased out. However, although some affected species recovered quickly, otter numbers did not and continued to fall into the 1980s. This was probably due mainly to habitat destruction and deaths on roads. Because otter populations had already been fragmented by the severe decline of the 1950s and 1960s, the loss of even a small number of animals in one area could make an entire local population unviable and lead to its disappearance.

G

Otter numbers have been recovering across Britain. Populations have grown in the few areas where they survived and have expanded from these centres into other parts of the country. This recovery is due largely to legislation, conservation measures, efforts to slow and reverse the destruction of suitable habitat, and the reintroduction of captive-bred animals. Releasing captive-bred otters is regarded by many conservationists as a last resort. The argument is that where suitable habitat does not exist, released animals will not survive, while where appropriate habitat is available, natural populations should eventually be able to expand into the area without assistance. However, introducing animals into a fragmented and fragile population may provide enough additional support for it to stabilise and expand rather than disappear. This was the approach taken by the Otter Trust in Norfolk, where the otter population may have fallen to as few as twenty animals at the beginning of the 1980s. The Otter Trust eventually ended its captive-breeding programme altogether—a positive development because it indicated that such intervention was no longer considered necessary.

parts.name: Passage 2
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Follow Your Nose

A

At the time of the research, aromatherapy was the most widely used complementary therapy in the National Health Service and was most commonly used in the treatment of dementia. For elderly patients who have difficulty interacting verbally and to whom conventional medicine has little to offer, aromatherapy can bring benefits in terms of better sleep, improved motivation and less disturbed behaviour. At least, that is the assumption. However, a systematic review of healthcare databases found almost no evidence that aromatherapy is effective in the treatment of dementia. Other findings suggest that aromatherapy may be effective only when patients believe that it will work. In fact, the only research that has unequivocally shown it to have an effect has been carried out on animals.

B

Behavioural studies have consistently shown that odours elicit emotional memories far more readily than other sensory cues. Rachel Herz, of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, and her colleagues used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine brain activity associated with this effect. They scanned the brains of five women while the participants either looked at a photograph of a bottle of perfume that evoked a pleasant memory for them or smelled the perfume itself. One woman, for instance, recalled that as a child living in Paris, she would watch with excitement as her mother dressed to go out and sprayed herself with the perfume. The women described the perfume as far more evocative than the photograph, and Herz and her colleagues found that the scent activated the amygdala and other brain regions associated with emotion processing far more strongly than the photograph. However, the odour did not enable the women to recall their memories in any greater detail or with greater clarity than the photograph did. “People don’t remember any more detail or with any more clarity when the memory is recalled with an odour,” Herz says. “However, with the odour, you have this intense emotional feeling that’s really visceral.”

C

This is hardly surprising, Herz argues, given how the brain has evolved. “The way I like to think about it is that emotion and olfaction are essentially the same things,” she says. “The part of the brain that controls emotion literally grew out of the part of the brain that controls smell.” She suggests that this may explain why memories associated with emotionally powerful odours become so deeply entrenched. Smell originally served a survival function, signalling whether something should be approached or avoided.

D

Eric Vermetten, a psychiatrist at the University of Utrecht in the Netherlands, says that doctors have long known about the potential of smells to act as traumatic reminders, although the evidence has been largely anecdotal. Vermetten and his colleagues attempted to document this effect by describing three cases of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in which patients reported either that a particular smell triggered their flashbacks or that smell was a feature of the flashback itself. The researchers concluded that odours could be used in exposure therapy or to recondition patients’ fear responses.

E

After Vermetten presented his findings at a conference, doctors in the audience described ways in which they had attempted to use this association therapeutically. PTSD patients often undergo group therapy, but the therapy itself can expose them to traumatic reminders. “Some clinicians put a strip of vanilla or a strong, pleasant, everyday odorant such as coffee under their patients’ noses, so that they have this continuous olfactory stimulation,” says Vermetten. With this continuous pleasant olfactory stimulus, patients appear to be better protected against flashbacks. The evidence is purely anecdotal, and nobody knows what is happening in the brain, Vermetten says. However, it is possible that the neural pathways through which the odour evokes a pleasant everyday memory override the fear-conditioned neural pathways that respond to verbal cues.

F

According to Herz, the therapeutic potential of odours could lie in their very unreliability. Her perfume-bottle experiment showed that odours do not produce more accurate or detailed recall, even when the memories they evoke feel more real. Research also shows that smell can be influenced because, as predominantly visual and verbal creatures, we tend to place greater trust in visual and verbal information. In 2001, for instance, Gil Morrot, of the National Institute for Agronomic Research in Montpellier, tricked 54 oenology students by secretly colouring a white wine with an odourless red dye just before they were asked to describe the odours of a range of red and white wines. The students described the coloured wine using terms typically reserved for red wines. They also used terms referring to the wine’s redness and darkness—visual rather than olfactory qualities. Smell, the researchers concluded, cannot be separated from the other senses.

G

In a later experiment, Jay Gottfried and Ray Dolan of the Wellcome Department of Imaging Neuroscience in London investigated how visual information affected the recognition of odours. They measured how quickly participants could identify an odour when it was accompanied either by a semantically related image or by an unrelated one, while their brains were scanned using fMRI. Participants might, for example, smell vanilla while seeing either a picture of ice cream or one of cheese. Participants identified the odours more quickly when the accompanying image was semantically related to the smell. When this occurred, a structure called the hippocampus was strongly activated. The researchers interpreted this as evidence that the hippocampus helps integrate information from different senses, which the brain then uses to determine what it is perceiving.

Follow Your Nose

A

At the time of the research, aromatherapy was the most widely used complementary therapy in the National Health Service and was most commonly used in the treatment of dementia. At least, that is the assumption. However, a systematic review of healthcare databases found almost no evidence that aromatherapy is effective in the treatment of dementia. Other findings suggest that aromatherapy may be effective only when patients believe that it will work. In fact, the only research that has unequivocally shown it to have an effect has been carried out on animals.

B

Behavioural studies have consistently shown that odours elicit emotional memories far more readily than other sensory cues. They scanned the brains of five women while the participants either looked at a photograph of a bottle of perfume that evoked a pleasant memory for them or smelled the perfume itself. One woman, for instance, recalled that as a child living in Paris, she would watch with excitement as her mother dressed to go out and sprayed herself with the perfume. The women described the perfume as far more evocative than the photograph, and Herz and her colleagues found that the scent activated the amygdala and other brain regions associated with emotion processing far more strongly than the photograph. parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3.

Grimm’s Fairy Tales

A

The Brothers Grimm, Jacob and Wilhelm, named their story collection Children’s and Household Tales and published the first of its seven editions in Germany in 1812. The table of contents reads like an A-list of fairy-tale celebrities: Cinderella, Sleeping Beauty, Snow White, Little Red Riding Hood, Rapunzel, Rumpelstiltskin, Hansel and Gretel, and the Frog King. Drawn mostly from oral narratives, the 210 stories in the Grimms’ collection represent an anthology of fairy tales, animal fables, rustic farces and religious allegories that remain unrivalled to this day.

B

Such lasting fame would have shocked the humble Grimms. During their lifetimes, the collection sold modestly in Germany, at first only a few hundred copies a year. The early editions were not even aimed at children. The brothers initially refused to consider illustrations, and scholarly footnotes took up almost as much space as the tales themselves. Jacob and Wilhelm viewed themselves as patriotic folklorists, not as children’s entertainers. They began their work at a time when Germany had been overrun by the French under Napoleon, who was intent on suppressing local culture. As young, workaholic scholars, single and sharing a cramped flat, the Brothers Grimm undertook the fairy-tale collection with the goal of preserving Germany’s endangered oral tradition.

C

For much of the 19th century, teachers, parents and religious figures, particularly in the United States, deplored the Grimms’ collection for its raw, uncivilised content. Offended adults objected to the gruesome punishments inflicted on the stories’ villains. In the original “Snow White”, the evil stepmother is forced to dance in red-hot iron shoes until she falls down dead. Even today, some protective parents shy away from the Grimms’ tales because of their reputation for violence.

D

Despite its sometimes rocky reception, Children’s and Household Tales gradually took root with the public. The brothers had not foreseen that the appearance of their work would coincide with a great flowering of children’s literature in Europe. English publishers led the way, issuing high-quality picture books such as Jack and the Beanstalk and handsome folktale collections, all to satisfy a newly literate audience seeking virtuous material for the nursery. Once the Brothers Grimm recognised this new readership, they set about refining and softening their tales, which had originated centuries earlier as earthy peasant fare. In the Grimms’ hands, cruel mothers became nasty stepmothers, unmarried lovers were made chaste, and the incestuous father was recast as the devil.

E

During the 20th century, the Grimms’ fairy tales came to dominate the bookshelves of children’s bedrooms. The stories read like dreams come true: handsome lads and beautiful damsels, armed with magic, triumph over giants, witches and wild beasts. They outwit mean, selfish adults. Inevitably, the boy and girl fall in love and live happily ever after. Parents also keep reading because they approve of the finger-wagging lessons inserted into the stories: keep your promises, don’t talk to strangers, work hard and obey your parents. According to the Grimms, the collection served as “a manual of manners”.

F

Altogether, some 40 people delivered tales to the Grimms. Many of the storytellers came to the Grimms’ house in Kassel. The brothers particularly welcomed the visits of Dorothea Viehmann, a widow who walked to town to sell produce from her garden. An innkeeper’s daughter, Viehmann had grown up listening to stories from travellers on the road to Frankfurt. Among her treasures was “Aschenputtel”—Cinderella. Marie Hassenpflug, a 20-year-old friend of their sister Charlotte, came from a well-bred, French-speaking family. Marie’s wonderful stories blended motifs from the oral tradition and from Perrault’s influential 1697 book, Tales of My Mother Goose, which contained elaborate versions of “Little Red Riding Hood”, “Snow White” and “Sleeping Beauty”, among others. Many of these had been adapted from earlier Italian tales.

G

Given that the origins of many of the Grimm fairy tales reach throughout Europe and into the Middle East and Asia, the question must be asked: How German are the Grimm tales? Very, says scholar Heinz Rolleke. Love of the underdog, rustic simplicity and creative energy—these are Teutonic traits. The coarse texture of life during medieval times in Germany, when many of the tales entered the oral tradition, also coloured the narratives. Throughout Europe, children were often neglected and abandoned, like Hansel and Gretel. Accused witches were burned at the stake, like the evil mother-in-law in “The Six Swans”. “The cruelty in the stories was not the Grimms’ fantasy,” Rolleke points out. “It reflected the law-and-order system of the old times.”

H

The editorial fingerprints left by the Grimms betray the specific values of 19th-century Christian, bourgeois German society. But that has not stopped the tales from being embraced by almost every culture and nationality in the world. What accounts for this widespread, enduring popularity? Bernhard Lauer points to the “universal style” of the writing: “You have no concrete descriptions of the land, or the clothes, or the forest, or the castles. It makes the stories timeless and placeless.” “The tales allow us to express our utopian longings,” says Jack Zipes of the University of Minnesota, whose 1987 translation of the complete fairy tales captures the rustic vigour of the original text. “They show a striving for happiness that none of us knows but that we sense is possible. We can identify with the heroes of the tales and become, in our minds, the masters and mistresses of our own destinies.”

I

Fairy tales provide a workout for the unconscious, psychoanalysts maintain. Bruno Bettelheim famously promoted the therapeutic value of the Grimms’ stories, calling fairy tales the “great comforters”. By confronting fears and phobias, symbolised by witches, heartless stepmothers and hungry wolves, children find they can master their anxieties. Bettelheim’s theory continues to be hotly debated. But most young readers are not interested in exercising their unconscious minds. The Grimm tales, in fact, please in an infinite number of ways. Something about them seems to mirror whatever moods or interests we bring to our reading of them. The flexibility of interpretation suits them for almost any time and any culture.

F

Altogether, some 40 people delivered tales to the Grimms. Many of the storytellers came to the Grimms’ house in Kassel. The brothers particularly welcomed the visits of Dorothea Viehmann, a widow who walked to town to sell produce from her garden. An innkeeper’s daughter, Viehmann had grown up listening to stories from travellers on the road to Frankfurt. Among her treasures was “Aschenputtel”—Cinderella. Marie Hassenpflug, a 20-year-old friend of their sister Charlotte, came from a well-bred, French-speaking family. Marie’s wonderful stories blended motifs from the oral tradition and from Perrault’s influential 1697 book, Tales of My Mother Goose, which contained elaborate versions of “Little Red Riding Hood”, “Snow White” and “Sleeping Beauty”, among others. Many of these had been adapted from earlier Italian tales.

G

Given that the origins of many of the Grimm fairy tales reach throughout Europe and into the Middle East and Asia, the question must be asked: How German are the Grimm tales? Very, says scholar Heinz Rolleke. Love of the underdog, rustic simplicity and creative energy—these are Teutonic traits. The coarse texture of life during medieval times in Germany, when many of the tales entered the oral tradition, also coloured the narratives. Throughout Europe, children were often neglected and abandoned, like Hansel and Gretel. Accused witches were burned at the stake, like the evil mother-in-law in “The Six Swans”. “The cruelty in the stories was not the Grimms’ fantasy,” Rolleke points out. “It reflected the law-and-order system of the old times.”

H

The editorial fingerprints left by the Grimms betray the specific values of 19th-century Christian, bourgeois German society. But that has not stopped the tales from being embraced by almost every culture and nationality in the world. What accounts for this widespread, enduring popularity? Bernhard Lauer points to the “universal style” of the writing: “You have no concrete descriptions of the land, or the clothes, or the forest, or the castles. It makes the stories timeless and placeless.” “The tales allow us to express our utopian longings,” says Jack Zipes of the University of Minnesota, whose 1987 translation of the complete fairy tales captures the rustic vigour of the original text. “They show a striving for happiness that none of us knows but that we sense is possible. We can identify with the heroes of the tales and become, in our minds, the masters and mistresses of our own destinies.”

I

Fairy tales provide a workout for the unconscious, psychoanalysts maintain. Bruno Bettelheim famously promoted the therapeutic value of the Grimms’ stories, calling fairy tales the “great comforters”. By confronting fears and phobias, symbolised by witches, heartless stepmothers and hungry wolves, children find they can master their anxieties. Bettelheim’s theory continues to be hotly debated. But most young readers are not interested in exercising their unconscious minds. The Grimm tales, in fact, please in an infinite number of ways. Something about them seems to mirror whatever moods or interests we bring to our reading of them. The flexibility of interpretation suits them for almost any time and any culture.
